options.text: Because Swift classes cannot conform to custom protocols.
options.explanation: Classes conform to protocols normally in Swift.

options.text: Because structs are cheap value types that SwiftUI recreates often.

options.text: Because structs allow multiple screens to share the same pointers.

questions.prompt: Explain why SwiftUI views are declared as structs instead of reference classes like UIView. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI views are lightweight descriptions of UI rather than persistent canvas objects.
Mentions that structs are stack-allocated value types with no reference counting overhead.
Explains that cheap recreation enables SwiftUI to rebuild and diff view hierarchies frequently.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI views are declarative descriptions of user interfaces, not persistent canvas objects like UIView. Because views are structs, they are allocated on the stack and avoid heap allocation and reference counting overhead. This lightweight nature allows SwiftUI to recreate view hierarchies cheaply whenever state changes. The framework then diffs the new struct tree against the old one to update the screen efficiently.

questions.prompt: Explain why the order of modifiers matters in SwiftUI, and give an example showing how reversing the order changes layout. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that modifiers do not mutate in place but wrap the view in a new container struct.
Gives an example comparing .padding().background() with .background().padding().
Describes the visual difference: coloring the expanded padded frame versus coloring only the tight text.

questions.modelAnswer: In SwiftUI, modifiers do not mutate an existing view. Instead, each modifier wraps the previous view into a new container struct. Because wrapping is hierarchical, order changes the layout. For example, calling .padding().background(.blue) expands the view frame first and paints the whole padded area blue. Reversing the order to .background(.blue).padding() paints only the tight text blue and leaves the outer padding transparent.

questions.prompt: What does the return type some View mean on the body property, and why is it used? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Identifies some View as an opaque return type introduced in Swift 5.1.
Explains that it hides complex nested generic modifier types (such as ModifiedContent).
Mentions that it preserves compile-time type safety while keeping code clean.

questions.modelAnswer: The body property returns some View, which is an opaque return type. Chaining view modifiers creates deeply nested generic types like ModifiedContent. Writing out these exact generic types would make view signatures unreadable and brittle. Using some View tells the compiler the property returns a specific concrete type. It hides messy generic details while maintaining full type safety.

questions.prompt: How do you build a custom ViewModifier in SwiftUI, and how do you make it easy to call? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Creates a struct conforming to the ViewModifier protocol.
Implements func body(content: Content) -> some View to style the incoming content.
Creates an extension on View to allow calling the modifier with dot syntax.

questions.modelAnswer: To build a custom modifier, declare a struct conforming to the ViewModifier protocol. Implement the required method func body(content: Content) -> some View, applying your desired styling to content. To make it easy to call, write an extension on View that wraps modifier(MyModifier()). This allows developers to apply the custom styling using standard dot-syntax chaining across any view.

questions.prompt: Why should you never execute slow tasks or network calls inside var body? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that var body is evaluated frequently on the main thread whenever state changes.
States that slow work blocks the main thread, leading to dropped frames and laggy UI.
Recommends initiating async work in appropriate lifecycle modifiers like .task or view models.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI evaluates var body frequently on the main thread whenever state or view dependencies update. Performing heavy tasks, synchronous file access, or network calls inside body blocks the main thread. This causes UI stutter, dropped frames, and unresponsive gestures. Instead, keep body purely declarative and start asynchronous work inside lifecycle modifiers like .task or inside view models.
